items.title: Urban Cooling
items.passage: Cities often plant trees to reduce summer heat. Tree canopies provide shade, while water released from leaves can cool the surrounding air. Yet planting programs do not automatically benefit every neighborhood. Wealthier districts may already have mature trees and enough space for new ones, whereas densely built areas often lack suitable land. Some cities therefore use heat maps and public-health data to identify blocks where additional shade could have the greatest effect. This approach can improve fairness, but it also requires long-term maintenance. Young trees need water and care for years before they provide substantial cooling.
items.prompt: Why do some cities use heat maps when planning tree programs?
choices: To identify places where shade is most needed
To measure the age of every tree
To determine which trees grow fastest
items.explanation: Answer from the passage; check the claim against the relevant sentence rather than relying on keywords.

items.title: Repairing Electronics
items.passage: Many electronic products are difficult to repair because components are glued together or replacement parts are unavailable. Supporters of right-to-repair rules argue that manufacturers should provide parts, tools, and manuals to consumers and independent repair shops. They say this could extend product life and reduce electronic waste. Manufacturers, however, warn that poorly performed repairs may create safety or cybersecurity risks. Some policymakers have responded by proposing rules that require access to repair information while allowing restrictions for genuinely sensitive components. The debate therefore concerns not simply whether repair is desirable, but how access can be expanded without creating new risks.
items.prompt: What is the central issue in the debate?
choices: How to expand repair access while managing risks
Whether manufacturers should stop publishing manuals
How to make products more expensive
items.explanation: Answer from the passage; check the claim against the relevant sentence rather than relying on keywords.

items.title: Citizen Science
items.passage: Professional researchers cannot always collect observations across a large geographic area for many years. Citizen-science projects address this limitation by asking volunteers to record information such as bird sightings, rainfall, or flowering dates. The resulting datasets can be enormous, but volunteer observations vary in accuracy. Researchers therefore design identification guides, training tasks, and statistical methods to reduce errors. When these safeguards are used, citizen science can reveal broad patterns that would otherwise be expensive to detect. It can also strengthen public interest in science, although participation may be uneven across regions and social groups.
items.prompt: Why are safeguards used in citizen-science projects?
choices: To reduce errors in volunteer observations
To prevent volunteers from seeing results
items.explanation: Answer from the passage; check the claim against the relevant sentence rather than relying on keywords.

items.title: Four-Day Workweek
items.passage: Trials of four-day workweeks have attracted attention from employers seeking to improve recruitment and reduce burnout. In many trials, employees receive the same pay while working fewer hours, so organizations must redesign meetings and workflows rather than simply compressing five days of tasks into four. Some companies report stable productivity and improved employee satisfaction. These findings, however, may not apply equally to hospitals, factories, or customer-service operations that require continuous coverage. Researchers therefore caution against treating the policy as a universal solution. Its success appears to depend on job design, staffing, and how productivity is measured.
items.prompt: What does the passage suggest is important for a successful four-day week?
choices: Simply doing five days of work in four
Redesigning work and considering job requirements
items.explanation: Answer from the passage; check the claim against the relevant sentence rather than relying on keywords.

items.title: AI and Hiring
items.passage: Employers increasingly use software to screen job applications. Automated tools can process large numbers of candidates quickly and may apply the same formal criteria to every application. Nevertheless, consistency does not guarantee fairness. If a system is trained on historical hiring decisions that reflect past inequalities, it may reproduce those patterns. In addition, applicants may not know why they were rejected. Some experts therefore recommend regular audits, documentation of selection criteria, and a meaningful way for candidates to request human review. Such measures do not eliminate every problem, but they can make automated hiring more accountable.
items.prompt: Why can an automated hiring system still be unfair?
choices: Historical data may contain past inequalities
items.explanation: Answer from the passage; check the claim against the relevant sentence rather than relying on keywords.

writing.source: Some cities have introduced shared bicycle systems to reduce car use. Supporters say the systems make short trips convenient and can connect commuters to railway stations. They may also reduce traffic and air pollution when people choose bicycles instead of cars. However, the programs are expensive to operate because bicycles must be repaired and redistributed among stations. In addition, usage often falls in bad weather, making revenue uncertain. Cities are experimenting with electric bicycles and better station placement to increase use.
writing.prompt: Summarize the passage in your own words. Aim for 60–70 words.

writing.source: Food-sharing applications connect stores and restaurants with customers willing to buy unsold food at a discount near closing time. The services can reduce food waste and allow consumers to purchase meals cheaply. Businesses may also recover some of the cost of products that would otherwise be discarded. Critics note, however, that users cannot always choose exactly what they receive and that collection times may be inconvenient. The applications also address surplus food after it has been produced rather than preventing overproduction in the first place.
